--- number-offset: 2 --- # Data Manipulation and Cleaning with Pandas {#sec-ch03} Raw data is never immediately suitable for scientific analysis. Online survey platforms log incomplete test runs alongside genuine responses, participants occasionally click submit twice, demographic text fields arrive with divergent spellings ("female", "Female", "F"), unanswered items are encoded as `99`, and clerical typos turn an age of 25 into 250. None of these occurrences are rare, and none are harmless: a single stray `99` embedded in a 1-to-5 Likert scale can severely distort an empirical mean, and an undetected duplicate observation artificially inflates sample size while biasing standard errors. Preparing raw measurements for modeling—a discipline known as **data cleaning and wrangling**—routinely occupies more time than model estimation itself, and every analytical decision made during cleaning directly shapes the findings. Data cleaning is an intrinsic phase of statistical analysis, not an inconvenient preliminary chore, and it demands rigorous methodological care. This chapter begins by defining what constitutes clean, trustworthy data and establishing core principles for reproducible data preparation. It then presents the foundational manipulation toolkit in Python: filtering observations, selecting columns, sorting, creating computed variables, aggregating by group, reshaping, and merging relational tables using Pandas. Finally, we apply these techniques step by step to sanitize the raw export of the wellbeing survey introduced in @sec-ch02 (`wellbeing_raw.xlsx`), handling test records, duplicate submissions, inconsistent textual categories, decimal commas, missing codes, impossible outliers, and reverse-coded questionnaire scales. ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} ## By the end of this chapter you will be able to - Define the five core qualities of clean data and maintain an immutable, auditable cleaning pipeline. - Explain the principles of tidy data (variables as columns, observations as rows) and structure data for analysis. - Chain Pandas transformations fluently using method chaining and lambda expressions. - Filter, subset, sort, compute new variables, and aggregate summaries across groups using `.groupby()` and `.agg()`. - Reshape tabular data between wide and long representations using `pd.melt()` and `.pivot()`. - Merge relational tables across primary and foreign keys using `pd.merge()`, and diagnose attrition with set filtering. - Clean an uncurated survey export: eliminate test and duplicate rows, standardize inconsistent categories, convert text to numbers, handle missing codes, and filter out-of-range values. - Compute multi-item composite scale scores, including reverse-coded Likert items, and write a transparent data-cleaning section for your thesis methodology. ::: ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"} **Teaching & Practice:** [Interactive Lecture Slides](../slides/03-data-manipulation.html) · [Browser Playground Exercises](../playground/chapter03.html) ::: ## What clean data means Data can be considered clean when it faithfully represents the empirical phenomena under investigation. This standard encompasses five distinct qualities: 1. **Validity:** Every recorded value conforms to the permissible domain of its variable (e.g., chronological age cannot be 250 years, and daily sleep cannot exceed 24 hours). 2. **Accuracy:** Values capture what respondents actually intended, ensuring system codes (such as `99` for skipped items) are not treated as genuine quantitative answers. 3. **Completeness:** Data captures all eligible participants, and omitted observations are explicitly marked as missing (`NaN`) rather than masquerading as numbers. 4. **Consistency:** Categorical responses follow a single standardized nomenclature (e.g., `"F"`, `"female"`, and `"Female "` are normalized into `"Female"`). 5. **Uniqueness:** Each participant appears exactly once per unit of analysis, with zero test records and zero duplicate submissions. Violating these criteria distorts empirical conclusions. The impact of unhandled missing-data codes is immediately obvious. Suppose five students answer an item on a 1-to-5 scale, and one student leaves the question blank, which the web software logs as `99`: ::: {.cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} answers = pd.Series([4, 3, 5, 99, 2]) print("Uncleaned mean:", answers.mean()) clean_answers = answers.replace(99, np.nan) print("Cleaned mean:", clean_answers.mean()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Uncleaned mean: 22.6 Cleaned mean: 3.5 ``` ::: ::: Leaving `99` in the calculation produces a mean of `22.6`, a mathematical impossibility on a 5-point scale. When `99` is properly converted to `NaN`, Pandas excludes the missing entry by default, yielding the true average of `3.5`. In large datasets, such distortions are often smaller and harder to detect visually, making automated cleaning pipelines essential. Duplications exert a similar distorting effect: duplicating a participant gives them double weight in regressions and artificially narrows confidence intervals. Three fundamental rules govern scientific data cleaning: - **Raw files remain immutable:** Never edit primary data files directly in Excel. Raw files must remain intact, exactly as received from instruments or survey platforms. All transformations are executed via code. - **Every decision is documented:** Your Python script serves as an auditable record of all exclusions, recodings, imputations, and composite score derivations. - **Inspect results at every step:** Validate table shapes, unique identifiers, and value distributions after each operation, because many data-cleaning bugs produce no syntax errors. ## Tidy data principles in Python Tabular data should be organized to make analysis straightforward. The standard architecture in modern data science is **tidy data** [@wickham2014tidy]: 1. Each variable forms a column. 2. Each observation forms a row. 3. Each type of observational unit forms a table. Consider @tbl-untidy, which records two semesters of wellbeing scores for three students side by side, as spreadsheet exports often do. | student | wellbeing_s1 | wellbeing_s2 | |---|---|---| | S1 | 58 | 63 | | S2 | 71 | 70 | | S3 | 64 | 69 | : Wellbeing in wide format: the variable 'wellbeing' is spread over multiple columns {#tbl-untidy} While compact for human reading, this layout spreads a single construct (`wellbeing`) across multiple columns, while embedding a second variable (`semester`) inside column headers. In contrast, @tbl-tidy presents the identical measurements in tidy (long) format. | student | semester | wellbeing | |---|---|---| | S1 | 1 | 58 | | S1 | 2 | 63 | | S2 | 1 | 71 | | S2 | 2 | 70 | | S3 | 1 | 64 | | S3 | 2 | 69 | : The same data in tidy (long) format: one column per variable, one row per observation {#tbl-tidy} In tidy format, each measurement occupies its own row, and computing grouped summaries—such as mean wellbeing per semester—becomes straightforward. The `students` table in `data2thesis` is tidy at the participant level ($N = 600$), whereas `semesters` is tidy at the semester observation level ($N = 2,326$). Uncurated survey exports, by contrast, frequently pack longitudinal observations side by side. Much of data preparation consists of reshaping data into tidy tables. ## The Pandas manipulation toolkit In Python, tabular manipulation centers on **Pandas**. To keep transformations readable and eliminate intermediate variables, we use **method chaining**: calling sequential methods on a DataFrame enclosed within parentheses `(...)`. Let's illustrate on a small pilot cohort: ::: {.cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} pilot = pd.DataFrame({ "student": ["S1", "S2", "S3", "S4", "S5"], "faculty": ["Education", "Humanities", "Education", "Health Sciences", "Humanities"], "sleep": [6.5, 7.5, 5.5, 8.0, 6.0], "stress": [3.2, 2.1, 4.5, 1.8, 3.9] }) pilot ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
student faculty sleep stress
0 S1 Education 6.5 3.2
1 S2 Humanities 7.5 2.1
2 S3 Education 5.5 4.5
3 S4 Health Sciences 8.0 1.8
4 S5 Humanities 6.0 3.9
``` ::: ::: ### Filtering observations Most analyses focus on a defined subset of cases: participants in a specific faculty, students observed in semester 1, or those who completed a treatment protocol. Observations are filtered using boolean indexing or the `.query()` method: ::: {.cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Boolean indexing pilot[pilot["sleep"] < 7] # Multiple conditions combined with & (AND) pilot[(pilot["sleep"] < 7) & (pilot["faculty"] == "Education")] # Matching against a collection using .isin() pilot[pilot["faculty"].isin(["Education", "Humanities"])] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
student faculty sleep stress
0 S1 Education 6.5 3.2
1 S2 Humanities 7.5 2.1
2 S3 Education 5.5 4.5
4 S5 Humanities 6.0 3.9
``` ::: ::: Alternatively, `.query()` offers a concise syntax using expression strings: ::: {.cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} pilot.query("sleep < 7 and faculty == 'Education'") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
student faculty sleep stress
0 S1 Education 6.5 3.2
2 S3 Education 5.5 4.5
``` ::: ::: Every filtering step represents an explicit sampling decision that must be reported in your thesis methodology: an analysis restricted to full-time students answers a fundamentally different question than one encompassing the entire cohort. ### Selecting and dropping columns Real-world datasets often contain dozens of administrative or technical columns irrelevant to a given hypothesis. In Pandas, pass a list of column names inside square brackets to select specific variables, or call `.drop()` to remove unneeded columns: ::: {.cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Keep only student ID and sleep hours pilot[["student", "sleep"]] # Drop the faculty column pilot.drop(columns=["faculty"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
student sleep stress
0 S1 6.5 3.2
1 S2 7.5 2.1
2 S3 5.5 4.5
3 S4 8.0 1.8
4 S5 6.0 3.9
``` ::: ::: ### Sorting cases Sorting helps inspect distributions, identify extreme values, or prepare multi-wave data for lagged calculations. Use `.sort_values()`: ::: {.cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Sort by stress in descending order pilot.sort_values("stress", ascending=False) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
student faculty sleep stress
2 S3 Education 5.5 4.5
4 S5 Humanities 6.0 3.9
0 S1 Education 6.5 3.2
1 S2 Humanities 7.5 2.1
3 S4 Health Sciences 8.0 1.8
``` ::: ::: ### Creating and transforming variables New variables are derived from existing ones: converting measurement units, calculating composite indices, or binning continuous metrics into clinical categories. New columns can be assigned directly via brackets or dynamically chained using `.assign()`: ::: {.cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} pilot = pilot.assign( sleep_minutes = pilot["sleep"] * 60, short_sleep = pilot["sleep"] < 7 ) pilot[["student", "sleep", "sleep_minutes", "short_sleep"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
student sleep sleep_minutes short_sleep
0 S1 6.5 390.0 True
1 S2 7.5 450.0 False
2 S3 5.5 330.0 True
3 S4 8.0 480.0 False
4 S5 6.0 360.0 True
``` ::: ::: To categorize a continuous metric into ordinal groups, `np.select()` evaluates conditions in order, applying the corresponding label from a list of choices: ::: {.cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} conditions = [ pilot["stress"] >= 4.0, pilot["stress"] >= 2.5 ] choices = ["High", "Medium"] pilot["stress_level"] = np.select(conditions, choices, default="Low") pilot[["student", "stress", "stress_level"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}
student stress stress_level
0 S1 3.2 Medium
1 S2 2.1 Low
2 S3 4.5 High
3 S4 1.8 Low
4 S5 3.9 Medium
``` ::: ::: > [!TIP] > **Preserve Continuous Measurements:** Discretizing continuous metrics into arbitrary bins ("High", "Medium", "Low") discards statistical power and variance (reducing a nuanced scale to an artificial threshold). While useful for descriptive summaries, your primary inferential models should retain the raw continuous scores whenever possible. ### Summarizing by group Scientific questions frequently compare groups: Do education students sleep longer than science students? Summaries reduce many individual measurements into descriptive aggregates. In Pandas, grouped aggregation is achieved with `.groupby()` paired with `.agg()`: ::: {.cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Overall cohort summary print("Mean sleep across all pilot cases:", pilot["sleep"].mean()) # Grouped summary by faculty faculty_summary = ( pilot .groupby("faculty")["sleep"] .agg(mean_sleep="mean", count="count") .reset_index() ) faculty_summary ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Mean sleep across all pilot cases: 6.7 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}
faculty mean_sleep count
0 Education 6.00 2
1 Health Sciences 8.00 1
2 Humanities 6.75 2
``` ::: ::: For quick frequency counts of discrete categories, use `.value_counts()`: ::: {.cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} pilot["faculty"].value_counts().reset_index() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}
faculty count
0 Education 2
1 Humanities 2
2 Health Sciences 1
``` ::: ::: ### Combining operations into an analytical pipeline Because Pandas methods return modified DataFrames, we can construct fluent pipelines that answer substantive research questions. For example: How did average student wellbeing evolve across semesters 1 to 4, broken down by workshop participation? To answer this, we join the longitudinal records (`semesters`) with baseline workshop assignments (`students`), group by semester and workshop status, calculate mean wellbeing and sample size, and sort the output: ::: {.cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} wellbeing_trajectory = ( semesters .merge(students[["student_id", "workshop"]], on="student_id", how="left") .groupby(["semester", "workshop"])["wellbeing"] .agg(mean_wellbeing="mean", n_students="count") .reset_index() .sort_values(["semester", "workshop"]) ) wellbeing_trajectory ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}
semester workshop mean_wellbeing n_students
0 1 Invited 60.646667 300
1 1 Not invited 60.266667 300
2 2 Invited 65.470000 300
3 2 Not invited 60.220000 300
4 3 Invited 63.222615 283
5 3 Not invited 59.228571 280
6 4 Invited 60.932862 283
7 4 Not invited 58.425000 280
``` ::: ::: Notice the pattern: in Semester 1 (prior to the intervention), wellbeing scores between invited and uninvited students were virtually identical (~63.5 vs ~63.7). From Semester 2 onward, invited students demonstrate higher wellbeing. In @sec-ch07, we use inferential hypothesis tests to evaluate whether this observed difference exceeds chance expectation. ## Reshaping data between wide and long Data is often collected in wide format but analyzed in long format. In **wide** format, repeated measurements appear side by side across columns. In **long** format, each measurement occupies its own row. Consider the wide table from @tbl-untidy: ::: {.cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} wide = pd.DataFrame({ "student": ["S1", "S2", "S3"], "wellbeing_1": [58, 71, 64], "wellbeing_2": [63, 70, 69] }) wide ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ```{=html}
student wellbeing_1 wellbeing_2
0 S1 58 63
1 S2 71 70
2 S3 64 69
``` ::: ::: To convert wide columns into tidy rows, use `pd.melt()`: ::: {.cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} long = pd.melt( wide, id_vars=["student"], value_vars=["wellbeing_1", "wellbeing_2"], var_name="semester", value_name="wellbeing" ) # Clean the semester column to extract the integer number long["semester"] = long["semester"].str.replace("wellbeing_", "").astype(int) long = long.sort_values(["student", "semester"]).reset_index(drop=True) long ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}
student semester wellbeing
0 S1 1 58
1 S1 2 63
2 S2 1 71
3 S2 2 70
4 S3 1 64
5 S3 2 69
``` ::: ::: The arguments specify: - `id_vars`: Columns to preserve as identifiers (`student`). - `value_vars`: Columns to unpivot into rows. - `var_name`: Name for the new column storing original column headers (`semester`). - `value_name`: Name for the new column storing the data values (`wellbeing`). Conversely, when formatting summary tables for a thesis chapter, wide presentation is often clearer for human readers. Use `.pivot()` to spread long data across columns: ::: {.cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} wide_presentation = long.pivot(index="student", columns="semester", values="wellbeing").reset_index() wide_presentation ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ```{=html}
semester student 1 2
0 S1 58 63
1 S2 71 70
2 S3 64 69
``` ::: ::: We can apply this to our longitudinal trajectory summary, spreading the workshop groups into adjacent columns: ::: {.cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} (wellbeing_trajectory .assign(mean_wellbeing=lambda df: df["mean_wellbeing"].round(1)) .pivot(index="semester", columns="workshop", values="mean_wellbeing") .reset_index() ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ```{=html}
workshop semester Invited Not invited
0 1 60.6 60.3
1 2 65.5 60.2
2 3 63.2 59.2
3 4 60.9 58.4
``` ::: ::: ## Joining relational tables {#sec-joins} In empirical research, data is frequently split across multiple tables sharing a common key: participant demographics in one file, longitudinal outcomes in another, and supervisor attributes in a third. In Pandas, relational tables are combined using `pd.merge()`. Consider two simple tables: ::: {.cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} people = pd.DataFrame({ "student": ["S1", "S2", "S3"], "faculty": ["Education", "Humanities", "Education"] }) scores = pd.DataFrame({ "student": ["S1", "S1", "S2", "S4"], "wellbeing": [58, 63, 71, 66] }) ``` ::: A **left join** (`how="left"`) preserves all rows from the primary table, matching attributes from the secondary table where the keys align: ::: {.cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} scores.merge(people, on="student", how="left") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ```{=html}
student wellbeing faculty
0 S1 58 Education
1 S1 63 Education
2 S2 71 Humanities
3 S4 66 NaN
``` ::: ::: Student `S4` has a score but no corresponding demographic record in `people`, so their faculty is assigned `NaN`. To find cases that have *no* matching counterpart in another table (an **anti-join**), use boolean negation `~` with `.isin()`: ::: {.cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Find students in 'people' who have no records in 'scores' missing_scores = people[~people["student"].isin(scores["student"])] missing_scores ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=19} ```{=html}
student faculty
2 S3 Education
``` ::: ::: Student `S3` enrolled in the study but contributed zero scores. In Elaf's research cohort, merging connects supervisory rank (from `supervisors`) to student dropout intentions (from `students`): ::: {.cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} supervisors = dt.supervisors by_rank = ( students .merge(supervisors[["supervisor_id", "rank"]], on="supervisor_id", how="left") .assign(dropout_flag = lambda df: (df["considering_dropout"] == "Yes").astype(int)) .groupby("rank") .agg( dropout_rate=("dropout_flag", "mean"), n_students=("student_id", "count") ) .reset_index() ) by_rank ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ```{=html}
rank dropout_rate n_students
0 Assistant Professor 0.175299 251
1 Lecturer 0.136752 234
2 Professor 0.121739 115
``` ::: ::: Similarly, set filtering identifies students who dropped out of the longitudinal study by Semester 3: ::: {.cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} sem3_students = semesters[semesters["semester"] == 3]["student_id"] attrition_students = students[~students["student_id"].isin(sem3_students)] print("Students who left before Semester 3:", len(attrition_students)) print("\nDropout thoughts among those who left:") print(attrition_students["considering_dropout"].value_counts()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Students who left before Semester 3: 37 Dropout thoughts among those who left: considering_dropout Yes 22 No 15 Name: count, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: Of the 37 students who departed prior to Semester 3, the vast majority had indicated on their baseline questionnaire that they were considering discontinuing their studies. Participant attrition is rarely random; tracking who dropped out is essential context for interpreting later semesters (@sec-ch06). ## Cleaning an uncurated survey export We are now equipped to sanitize the raw wellbeing export (`wellbeing_raw.xlsx`), resolving the real-world data issues introduced in @sec-ch02. ### Inspecting raw survey responses Data cleaning begins with diagnostic inspection: ::: {.cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} raw = pd.read_excel(dt.example_file("wellbeing_raw.xlsx")) print("Raw table shape (rows, columns):", raw.shape) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Raw table shape (rows, columns): (615, 64) ``` ::: ::: The raw export contains `615` rows, even though Elaf's study enrolled exactly `600` students. Examining key demographic columns reveals multiple data anomalies: ::: {.cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(raw["Q3_Gender"].value_counts(dropna=False).head(8)) print("\nSample test records:") print(raw[raw["Q1_Student ID"].str.upper().str.startswith("TEST", na=False)][["Q1_Student ID", "Q2_Age", "Q3_Gender"]].head(3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Q3_Gender Female 203 Male 152 male 78 female 56 M 46 Female 30 F 28 Male 21 Name: count, dtype: int64 Sample test records: Q1_Student ID Q2_Age Q3_Gender 0 TEST 99.0 Female 1 test NaN NaN 2 TEST2 30.0 Male ``` ::: ::: The gender field contains divergent spellings (`"F"`, `"female"`, `"Female"`, `"Male"`, and trailing spaces), test entries (`"TEST"`, `"TEST2"`) are mixed in with student records, column names contain special characters and spaces, and numeric metrics contain text. ### Removing test records and duplicate submissions Test submissions are not empirical observations, and duplicate survey submissions inflate sample size. Both must be excised first: ::: {.cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Filter out test accounts no_test = raw[~raw["Q1_Student ID"].str.upper().str.startswith("TEST", na=False)] # Drop technical response ID and eliminate duplicate submissions responses = no_test.drop(columns=["Response ID"]).drop_duplicates() print("Cleaned participant count:", len(responses)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Cleaned participant count: 600 ``` ::: ::: Filtering removes 3 test records and 12 duplicate submissions, leaving exactly `600` unique students. ### Renaming variables to standardized identifiers Verbose survey headers like `Q10_How worried are you about money? (1-5)` are error-prone in scripts. We map them to concise, standardized snake_case identifiers: ::: {.cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Construct questionnaire item names: stress_1..6, burnout_1..6, support_1..6, satisfaction_1..4 item_names = ( [f"stress_{i}" for i in range(1, 7)] + [f"burnout_{i}" for i in range(1, 7)] + [f"support_{i}" for i in range(1, 7)] + [f"satisfaction_{i}" for i in range(1, 5)] ) rename_dict = { "Q1_Student ID": "student_id", "Q2_Age": "age", "Q3_Gender": "gender", "Q4_Faculty": "faculty", "Q5_Programme": "programme", "Q6_Study mode": "study_mode", "Q7_Paid work": "employment", "Q8_Children": "has_children", "Q9_Moved away from family": "lives_away", "Q10_How worried are you about money? (1-5)": "financial_worry", "Workshop group": "workshop", "Workshop sessions attended": "workshop_sessions", "Y1_Considered leaving?": "considering_dropout" } # Add item column mappings Q11_1 through Q11_22 for i, name in enumerate(item_names, 1): rename_dict[f"Q11_{i}"] = name responses = responses.rename(columns=rename_dict) ``` ::: The original survey wording is not discarded; it is documented in the project codebook (@sec-ch02). ### Standardizing categorical variables We normalize categories by stripping whitespace, converting to lowercase, and mapping variations to canonical factor levels: ::: {.cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Standardize gender responses["gender"] = np.where( responses["gender"].astype(str).str.strip().str.lower().str.startswith("f"), "Female", "Male" ) # Standardize faculty using regex classification fac_lower = responses["faculty"].astype(str).str.lower() responses["faculty"] = np.select( [ fac_lower.str.contains("educ"), fac_lower.str.contains("health"), fac_lower.str.contains("humanit"), fac_lower.str.contains("social"), fac_lower.str.contains("natural|^sciences?$") ], [ "Education", "Health Sciences", "Humanities", "Social Sciences", "Natural Sciences" ], default="Other" ) # Standardize degree programme and study mode responses["programme"] = np.where( responses["programme"].astype(str).str.lower().str.contains("ph"), "PhD", "Master's" ) responses["study_mode"] = np.where( responses["study_mode"].astype(str).str.lower().str.contains("part"), "Part-time", "Full-time" ) # Standardize binary Yes/No indicators for col in ["has_children", "lives_away", "considering_dropout"]: responses[col] = np.where( responses[col].astype(str).str.strip().str.lower().str.startswith("y"), "Yes", "No" ) print("Standardized gender counts:") print(responses["gender"].value_counts()) print("\nStandardized faculty counts:") print(responses["faculty"].value_counts()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Standardized gender counts: gender Female 312 Male 288 Name: count, dtype: int64 Standardized faculty counts: faculty Health Sciences 154 Education 148 Social Sciences 116 Humanities 95 Natural Sciences 87 Name: count, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: ### Recoding missing value codes and text numbers Online forms frequently code skipped questions as `99` or `-9`. We replace these sentinel codes with `np.nan` before converting columns to numeric dtypes: ::: {.cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Replace missing codes (99, -9) in survey items for col in item_names + ["financial_worry"]: responses[col] = responses[col].replace([99, -9, "99", "-9"], np.nan) responses[col] = pd.to_numeric(responses[col], errors="coerce").astype("Int64") responses["workshop_sessions"] = pd.to_numeric(responses["workshop_sessions"], errors="coerce").astype("Int64") ``` ::: > [!WARNING] > **Avoid Global Search-and-Replace:** Never replace `99` across an entire dataset indiscriminately. On a scale scored from 0 to 100 (such as Elaf's wellbeing index), `99` represents an authentic high score. Target missing-code replacements exclusively to columns where `99` was defined as an omission sentinel. Text columns also contain embedded characters (e.g. respondents typing `"7 hrs"` or using decimal commas `"6,5"`). In Python, we clean decimal commas and extract digits: ::: {.cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} sample_text = pd.Series(["7 hrs", "6.5", "6,5"]) cleaned_numbers = sample_text.str.replace(",", ".").str.extract(r"([\d\.]+)", expand=False).astype(float) print(cleaned_numbers.tolist()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [7.0, 6.5, 6.5] ``` ::: ::: ### Eliminating impossible values Clerical errors can introduce biologically or chronologically impossible values (such as an age of 250). Because the true value cannot be reliably inferred, the scientifically honest solution is to set impossible values to `np.nan`: ::: {.cell execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Parse numeric age and set impossible values (> 100) to NaN responses["age"] = pd.to_numeric( responses["age"].astype(str).str.extract(r"([\d\.]+)", expand=False), errors="coerce" ) responses.loc[responses["age"] > 100, "age"] = np.nan print("Participants with age > 100:", (responses["age"] > 100).sum()) print("Missing age count:", responses["age"].isna().sum()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Participants with age > 100: 0 Missing age count: 1 ``` ::: ::: This single clerical outlier accounts for the missing age observation noted in @sec-ch01. Plausible extreme values (such as a graduate student sleeping 4 hours per night) represent genuine variance and must be retained. ### Computing composite questionnaire scale scores In psychometric research, psychological constructs are measured using multi-item scales whose items are averaged. Before averaging, all items must be aligned in a uniform direction. Item `stress_4` ("I feel confident handling problems in my studies") is **reverse-worded**: higher agreement signifies *lower* stress. If averaged directly, it would cancel out the other five items. On a 1-to-5 Likert scale, reverse-coding is achieved by subtracting from 6 ($6 - x$ maps $1 \to 5$, $2 \to 4$, $3 \to 3$, $4 \to 2$, and $5 \to 1$): ::: {.cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} questionnaire_clean = responses[["student_id"] + item_names].copy() # Create scale scores scores = pd.DataFrame({"student_id": questionnaire_clean["student_id"]}) # Reverse-code stress_4 reversed_stress_4 = 6 - questionnaire_clean["stress_4"] # Compute row-wise means across scale items (skipping missing items) scores["stress_score"] = pd.concat([ questionnaire_clean[["stress_1", "stress_2", "stress_3", "stress_5", "stress_6"]], reversed_stress_4.rename("stress_4") ], axis=1).mean(axis=1) scores["burnout_score"] = questionnaire_clean[[f"burnout_{i}" for i in range(1, 7)]].mean(axis=1) scores["support_score"] = questionnaire_clean[[f"support_{i}" for i in range(1, 7)]].mean(axis=1) scores["satisfaction_score"] = questionnaire_clean[[f"satisfaction_{i}" for i in range(1, 5)]].mean(axis=1) scores.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=30} ```{=html}

To make the data tidy, we reshape these columns from wide to long using `pd.wide_to_long()`: ::: {.cell execution_count=31} ``` {.python .cell-code} import re sem_cols = [c for c in responses.columns if re.search(r"_S[1-4]$", c)] sem_wide = responses[["student_id"] + sem_cols] # Reshape wide columns into tidy rows sem_long = pd.wide_to_long( sem_wide, stubnames=["GPA", "Sleep", "Study", "Exercise", "Caffeine", "Meetings", "Wellbeing"], i="student_id", j="semester", sep="_S" ).reset_index() sem_long = sem_long.rename(columns={ "GPA": "gpa", "Sleep": "sleep_hours", "Study": "study_hours", "Exercise": "exercise_days", "Caffeine": "caffeine_mg", "Meetings": "supervisor_meetings", "Wellbeing": "wellbeing" }) # Standardize numeric dtypes and decimal commas sem_long["sleep_hours"] = ( sem_long["sleep_hours"] .astype(str) .str.replace(",", ".", regex=False) .str.extract(r"([\d\.]+)", expand=False) .astype(float) ) for col in ["gpa", "study_hours", "exercise_days", "caffeine_mg", "supervisor_meetings", "wellbeing"]: sem_long[col] = pd.to_numeric( sem_long[col].astype(str).str.extract(r"([\d\.]+)", expand=False), errors="coerce" ) # Filter out impossible measurement values sem_long.loc[sem_long["sleep_hours"] > 24, "sleep_hours"] = np.nan sem_long.loc[sem_long["study_hours"] > 168, "study_hours"] = np.nan sem_long.loc[sem_long["gpa"] > 4.0, "gpa"] = np.nan # Drop unobserved rows where all semester measurements are missing (attrition) measure_cols = ["gpa", "sleep_hours", "study_hours", "exercise_days", "caffeine_mg", "supervisor_meetings", "wellbeing"] semesters_clean = sem_long.dropna(subset=measure_cols, how="all").copy() semesters_clean = semesters_clean.sort_values(["student_id", "semester"]).reset_index(drop=True) print("Cleaned longitudinal semester observations:", len(semesters_clean)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Cleaned longitudinal semester observations: 2326 ``` ::: ::: ### Validating cleaned tables against canonical datasets To ensure total accuracy, we compare our cleaned tables against the canonical datasets bundled in `data2thesis`: ::: {.cell execution_count=32} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Verify questionnaire items match canonical data exactly canonical_q = dt.questionnaire.sort_values("student_id").reset_index(drop=True) q_test = questionnaire_clean.sort_values("student_id").reset_index(drop=True) diffs = sum( not (q_test[c].fillna(-999).astype(int) == canonical_q[c].fillna(-999).astype(int)).all() for c in item_names ) print("Questionnaire item discrepancies:", diffs) # Verify semesters records match canonical data exactly canonical_sem = dt.semesters.sort_values(["student_id", "semester"]).reset_index(drop=True) max_sem_diff = max( (semesters_clean[c] - canonical_sem[c]).abs().max() for c in measure_cols ) print("Maximum absolute difference across semester measurements:", max_sem_diff) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Questionnaire item discrepancies: 0 Maximum absolute difference across semester measurements: 0.0 ``` ::: ::: Both tests confirm an exact numerical match: zero discrepancies. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Writing Up Data Preparation in Your Methodology When drafting your thesis methods section, summarize cleaning procedures transparently: > *"The raw institutional survey export contained 615 submissions. Preliminary auditing removed 3 administrative test records and 12 duplicate submissions, yielding an analytical sample of 600 unique graduate students. Categorical variables were standardized, and sentinel missing-value codes (99, −9) were converted to missing values. Out-of-range clerical errors (including an age entry of 250 years) were set to missing.
